sents.text: Every file on Linux belongs to someone, and comes with rules about who can read it, change it or run it.
Most permission denied errors you'll ever see come from these rules.
Today you learn to read them and change them.
Linux is built for many people sharing one machine.
Each person has a user account.
Users can belong to groups, like a team.
And one special user, root, is the administrator, who can do anything.
Every file has one owner user and one owner group.
Run ls dash l, and the first column is the permission string.
The first character is the type: a dash for a file, d for a directory.
Then come three groups of three letters: for the owner, for the group, and for everyone else.
After that you see the owner's name, the group's name, the size, and the file name.
r is read: see what's inside.
x is execute: for a file, run it as a program; for a folder, enter it with cd.
A dash means that permission is missing.
So r w x, r dash x, r dash dash means: the owner can do everything, the group can read and run, and everyone else can only read.
